dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Greg.

Hi, yeah, hi, my name is Isabel Costa, I rent at 28 Old Beach Road, down by Easton's Beach, and my landlord said he wants to build a second-story deck off the back and he said I should call and find out about the railing height and whatever else, because I'm the one who's home, and I wasn't sure if it's you or the building people, and also the wind last weekend with that nor'easter, Saturday into Sunday, kind of messed with the back stairs so he wants to do it now, so, um, what do I need to know?
Okay, slow down a second. You're in the right place. A second-story deck, that's a deck permit. Is your landlord the owner on record?
Yeah, he's the owner. I'm just, I'm the renter. Is it a deck permit or a building permit? Because he said two different things.
It's a building permit, the type is deck. Same thing. The owner or his contractor files it, not you.
Oh. [line breaks up] okay so he has to do it, not me. And the railing, how high does it have to be? I thought it was thirty-six inches but my cousin said forty-two.

You're not far off. Thirty-six is common for a lot of residential decks, but I don't want you going off a guess. Elevated decks have guard requirements, and the inspector goes by the code that's adopted. The permit application will spell it out, and the plan reviewer will tell him if the drawing's wrong.
So thirty-six or forty-two, you're, sorry, you're saying it could be either?
I'm saying don't buy lumber until the plans are approved. Whatever number is on the approved plan, that's what gets built.
Okay. Okay. And is there an inspection? Like does somebody come out, or is it just the permit and then he builds it?
Yes, there are inspections. Usually one when the footings go in, one for the framing before it's covered up, and a final. He calls to schedule them as he goes.
Wait, footings, that's the, the posts in the ground? [inaudible] Sorry, you cut out. It's a second story so is it on posts or attached to the house?
Could be both. If it's attached to the house, there's a ledger connection the inspector looks at. Either way it goes on the drawing. Your landlord or whoever he hires can sort that out.
Right, okay. Because I'm, I actually apprentice with a roofer, and I have a ladder lesson at one today, so I kind of know ladders, but not decks, and I told him I'd ask.
Well, good. Then you'll want to make sure nobody's working off a ladder without a permit on the wall. Is that a yes on him filing?
I think so? I mean, he has to come in, you said, or can he do it from, um, somewhere else? I'm sorry, I don't totally get the process.

He can come to the office on Broadway, or call and we'll walk him through what to bring. Site plan, drawings, and who's doing the work. Want me to put a note with your name and address that you called?
Yes, please. Isabel Costa, 28 Old Beach Road. And if he has questions he can call me, it's 401-555-0151.
Got it. I'll note that. Tell him to call this office before he does anything.
Okay, thank you. So permit first, then the three inspections, and the railing is on the plans. Is that right?
That's it. Permit, inspections as he goes, railing per the approved plan.
Okay. Thanks, Greg. I think I got it. Mostly.
Any time. Good luck with the ladder.
